solutions.check: grid and clues read from the FT's printable PDF, its numbering matching the clue list; every fifteensquared answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Pass towards goal followed by save? It's above the keeper's head

parts.note: in football a cross is a pass played from the wing into the goalmouth
save in the sense 'except' is bar, as in 'all bar one'

explanation.surface: A football commentator describes a cross into the box and a save, then notes something over the goalkeeper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'save' looks like a goalkeeper's stop, but here it means 'except'.
explanation.definitionFit: The horizontal top of the goal frame sits directly over the goalkeeper standing on the line.

clue.text: Metal detector finally found in house after century

indicators.note: after means the house comes after the century letter

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred, a century

indicators.note: in means the last letter goes inside the house word

parts.note: a home is a house

indicators.note: finally picks the last letter of the word detector

explanation.surface: A metal detector finally finds something in an old house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Metal detector' reads as one gadget, but 'Metal' is the definition and 'detector finally' gives R.
explanation.definitionFit: Chrome is chromium, a hard shiny metallic element used for plating.

clue.text: Only half obtain benefit? That's stupid

indicators.note: only half takes the first three of the six letters of obtain

parts.note: use means benefit, as in 'of no use'

explanation.surface: Someone scoffs at getting only half the benefit they are owed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Only half' keeps OBT, the first half of 'obtain'.
explanation.definitionFit: An obtuse person is slow to understand, dim-witted.

clue.text: Intended recipient of my work, so to speak, in Chesterfield?

definitions.text: Intended recipient of my work, so to speak

explanation.surface: The setter wonders who their puzzle is for, in a town in Derbyshire.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter speaks as 'my': one who sets is a setter, so the person set to becomes, by the same suffix as employee, a 'settee'. A Chesterfield is a deep-buttoned leather sofa, not only an English town.
explanation.definitionFit: A mock word for the solver who receives what the compiler sets, and a long upholstered seat for two or more people.

clue.text: Sailor runs off into the water, honest

parts.note: AB, able seaman, is a sailor

indicators.note: off means taken away from the phrase for falling into the water

parts.note: someone going overboard ends up in the water
R is the cricket abbreviation for runs

explanation.surface: A sailor flees and dives into the sea, proving himself honest.
explanation.walkthrough: OVERBOARD loses R ('runs off') to give OVEBOARD. In cricket R stands for runs.
explanation.definitionFit: Above-board dealings are open and legitimate, with nothing concealed.

clue.text: Dropping temperature killed labiate plant

indicators.note: killed works as a word for something destroyed and so put into a new disorder
dropping means a letter is let go from the word that follows

explanation.surface: A labiate plant dies when the thermometer falls.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dropping' takes T out of LABIATE, leaving LABIAE, and 'killed' rearranges those six letters. Labiate is a real botanical word, for the mint family, which helps the disguise.
explanation.definitionFit: Abelia is a flowering shrub of the honeysuckle family, a garden plant.

clue.text: Architect supporting France's fine and dandy

indicators.note: supporting in a down answer means the architect goes below the French word

parts.note: beau is French for fine or handsome
John Nash was the architect of Regency London, including Regent Street

explanation.surface: An architect backs France's fine and dandy approach.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fine and dandy' looks like one phrase; 'dandy' is the definition. In a down answer 'supporting' puts NASH under BEAU.
explanation.definitionFit: Richard 'Beau' Nash was the eighteenth-century leader of fashion in Bath, a famous fop.

clue.text: Los Angeles, and all freaking out in intoxicated state

indicators.note: freaking out suggests going wild, so the letters are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: Everyone in Los Angeles is freaking out while drunk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'freaking out' rearranges AND ALL into LALAND. 'Los Angeles' is also what the answer nicknames, which adds to the joke.
explanation.definitionFit: La-la land is a dreamy, unreal frame of mind, as if high or drunk; it is also a nickname for Los Angeles.

clue.text: Worried about rent over year? One can help in case

indicators.note: over in a down answer means this part sits above the year
about means the worry word goes around the torn word

parts.note: something that ate at you worried you
rent means torn, as in a garment rent apart

explanation.surface: A tenant fretting about rent going up over the year looks for help in a legal case.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rent' looks like money paid to a landlord but means torn. ATE goes 'about' TORN to give ATTORNE, and 'over' puts that above Y.
explanation.definitionFit: A lawyer, especially in the US, represents a client in a court case.

clue.text: For example Radio 3 needs no introduction after end of Wagner Ring Cycle

indicators.note: end of picks out the final letter of the composer's name that follows

parts.note: a ring is round, the shape of the letter O

indicators.note: needs no introduction means the first letter is dropped

parts.note: BBC Radio 3 is an example of a radio station

explanation.surface: A music lover notes that a famous radio channel hardly needs presenting before Wagner's great opera cycle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wagner Ring Cycle' reads as the opera cycle, but it splits into R, O and the definition. Radio 3 is the BBC's classical music station, and 'needs no introduction' removes its first letter, leaving TATION.
explanation.definitionFit: A rotation is a turning round in a complete circle, a cycle.

clue.text: Labour's rejected by a great many in election

indicators.note: rejected means turned back, so the party's short form is read backwards

parts.note: Lab is the usual short form of the British Labour Party
'a lot' means a great many

explanation.surface: Labour loses an election when many voters turn against it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rejected' reverses LAB to BAL. 'a great many' is 'a lot', and the 'a' does its work there and nowhere else.
explanation.definitionFit: A ballot is a secret vote, the means by which an election is held.

clue.text: French composer's sestet regularly included by French artist

indicators.note: included by means the letters go inside the painter's name

parts.note: Edouard Manet was a French painter

indicators.note: regularly takes every other letter of the word sestet

explanation.surface: A French painter takes a six-line poem by a French composer into his work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'regularly' takes the first, third and fifth letters of 'sestet', giving SSE, and 'included by' puts them inside MANET. The 's after 'composer' stands for 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Jules Massenet was the nineteenth-century composer of the operas Manon and Werther.

clue.text: One hoping for a catch from spin bowler at last

parts.note: to spin a story is to angle it, give it a slant

indicators.note: at last picks the final letter of the word bowler

explanation.surface: A cricket fielder hopes to take a catch off a spin bowler.
explanation.walkthrough: The cricket picture of spin bowling and catches is a decoy: 'spin' means slant, ANGLE, and the catch is a fish.
explanation.definitionFit: A fisherman with rod and line hopes to land a fish.

clue.text: Penniless daughter's to have dole, but not husband

parts.note: D is the abbreviation for daughter; the 's means 'is'
to own is to have

indicators.note: but not means a letter is left out of the gift word

parts.note: a handout is a dole, a charitable gift

explanation.surface: A daughter must live on benefits since there is no husband to support her.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dole' suggests the British state unemployment benefit, but here it is a HANDOUT, which loses H for husband.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone down-and-out is destitute and homeless, without money.

clue.text: Duplicated one's new novel, being sensible

indicators.note: novel means new and strange, so the letters are put into a fresh order
duplicated means the following letters are taken twice over

parts.note: taken as the letters ONES, with the apostrophe ignored

explanation.surface: Someone praises a copied novel as sensible.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Duplicated' doubles ONES plus N to give ONESNONESN, and 'novel' rearranges those ten letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A no-nonsense person is practical and down-to-earth, without frills.

clue.text: Island mountain I'd rashly climb without covering

indicators.note: climb in a down answer means the letters read upwards
without covering means the outer parts of the phrase are stripped, leaving inner letters

explanation.surface: Someone foolishly scales an island peak with no protection.
explanation.walkthrough: AINIDRAS sits inside 'mountain I'd rashly' once the outer letters are stripped, and 'climb' reads it upwards in the down answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Sardinia is the large Italian Mediterranean territory surrounded by sea, west of the mainland.

clue.text: Under interrogation sounded mendacious — that's not unknown for traitor

indicators.note: sounded means the word is given as it is spoken

parts.note: to be quizzed is to be under interrogation, so quiz stands for it

indicators.note: not means a letter is removed from the word for mendacious

parts.note: lying means mendacious
Y is one of the letters used for an unknown quantity in algebra

explanation.surface: A suspect under questioning seemed to be lying, which shows they are a traitor.
explanation.walkthrough: QUIZ said aloud gives QUIS, and LYING without Y (an algebraic unknown) gives LING.
explanation.definitionFit: Vidkun Quisling led Norway's Nazi puppet government, and his name came to mean a collaborator.

clue.text: To cheer me up, thick type starts to explain Nietzsche

indicators.note: up in a down answer means the word is read upwards

parts.note: bold is thick type in printing

indicators.note: starts to picks the first letters of the two words that follow

explanation.surface: To cheer me up, a philosophy book prints a heavy-type introduction to Nietzsche.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' reverses ME to EM. 'starts to explain Nietzsche' gives E and N.
explanation.definitionFit: To embolden is to encourage, giving someone courage and heart.

clue.text: Colour as worn by a serviceman? On the contrary

indicators.note: worn by would put the word for 'as' around the serviceman, as clothes go around a body
on the contrary reverses the previous instruction, so the serviceman goes around the word for 'as'

parts.note: a marine is a soldier serving at sea
qua is Latin-derived English for 'as' or 'in the capacity of'

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a colour is the one a serviceman wears.
explanation.walkthrough: Clothes go round the wearer, so 'worn by' alone would put the 'as' word outside; 'On the contrary' flips that. 'serviceman' could be soldier or sailor; the marine fits the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Aquamarine is a pale blue-green shade named after the gemstone.

clue.text: Cleric I encountered in book store

indicators.note: encountered in means the letter is met with inside the other letters

parts.note: a shop is a store

explanation.surface: A churchman says he met someone in a bookshop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'book store' reads as one place, but it splits into B and SHOP with I placed between them.
explanation.definitionFit: A bishop is a senior clergyman in charge of a diocese.

clue.text: Iron Lady's capital investment?

parts.note: Fe is the chemical symbol for iron
Dora is a woman's name, standing for any lady; the 's means 'is'

explanation.surface: It asks whether the Iron Lady, Margaret Thatcher, put money into the City.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Iron Lady' suggests Margaret Thatcher. 'capital' means head, and 'investment' means clothing, so a capital investment is a hat.
explanation.definitionFit: A fedora is a soft felt hat, something you put on your head.

clue.text: She needs propitiatory gift to hurry

parts.note: a sop is something given to pacify or appease
hie is an old word meaning to hurry

explanation.surface: A woman needs a peace offering in a hurry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'She' is the definition: the answer is a woman's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Sophie is a girl's name, so the pronoun stands for any woman of that name.

clue.text: Democrat wants extraordinary powers returned to dictator

parts.note: ESP, extrasensory perception, is a supposed extraordinary mental power

indicators.note: returned means the little word that follows is read backwards

explanation.surface: A Democrat seizes emergency powers and becomes a dictator.
explanation.walkthrough: 'returned' reverses 'to', giving OT. 'extraordinary powers' looks like emergency government powers but is ESP.
explanation.definitionFit: A despot is an absolute ruler who uses power cruelly, a tyrant.

clue.text: Unsympathetic character in drama playing on the air

indicators.note: playing means the letters perform in a fresh arrangement

explanation.surface: A villainous character is performed on radio.
explanation.walkthrough: 'playing on the air' looks like a radio broadcast; 'playing' rearranges ONTHEAIR.
explanation.definitionFit: An antihero is a protagonist who lacks heroic qualities.

clue.text: Legendary swimmers from Norway are involved in relief heading for Somalia

parts.note: N is the international vehicle code for Norway

indicators.note: involved in means the unit's letter goes inside the word for relief

parts.note: aid means relief, as in famine relief
an are is a metric unit of area, abbreviated A

indicators.note: heading for picks the first letter of the following word

explanation.surface: Norway joins a famine relief effort for Somalia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'are' is the metric unit of area, A, which goes into AID to make AIAD.
explanation.definitionFit: Naiads are water nymphs of Greek myth who live in springs and rivers.

clue.text: Ring about dog losing collar, initially getting ridicule

indicators.note: about means turned around, so the ring word is read backwards

parts.note: a hoop is a ring

indicators.note: losing means a letter is taken away from the dog word

parts.note: a pooch is an informal word for a dog

indicators.note: initially picks the first letter of the word collar

explanation.surface: A dog slips its collar and gets laughed at.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' reverses HOOP to POOH, and POOCH 'losing' C ('collar, initially') gives the second POOH.
explanation.definitionFit: To pooh-pooh something is to dismiss it with scorn, deriding it.

clue.text: Articles about drink causing disease

indicators.note: about means the two articles go around the drink

parts.note: an is the indefinite article before a vowel
a is the indefinite article
gin is a drink

explanation.surface: A newspaper blames certain items about drinking for causing illness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Articles' gives two pieces, AN and A, which go 'about' GIN.
explanation.definitionFit: Angina is chest pain caused by poor blood flow to the heart, a medical condition.

clue.text: Post is disrupted by call for strike

indicators.note: disrupted means the four letters are thrown into a new order

parts.note: to page someone is to call them over a speaker

explanation.surface: Mail is held up by a call for industrial action.
explanation.walkthrough: 'disrupted' rearranges POST into STOP. The postal-strike picture hides that 'call' is PAGE.
explanation.definitionFit: A stoppage is a halt to work by employees, an industrial strike.
